\documentclass{article}
\title{Export Concentration and Growth Volatility: A Panel Reassessment}
\author{S. Mensah}
\date{}
\begin{document}
\maketitle

\section{Introduction}
A recurring finding in the development literature is that export
concentration amplifies output volatility in small open economies.
\cite{deng2023} estimate that a one-standard-deviation rise in product
concentration raises the variance of GDP growth by about eight percent
in their sample of Sub-Saharan economies. The result has been influential
in the policy debate, but the panel ends in 2011 and predates the
commodity price collapse that dominates the following decade.

This paper reassesses the finding on an extended panel that runs to
2022. We keep the specification of the original study as close as
possible so that differences in the estimates can be attributed to the
sample rather than to modelling choices.

\section{Empirical strategy}
Following \cite{deng2023}, we instrument export concentration with
the interaction of colonial-era port locations and world commodity
prices. The identifying assumption is that port geography affects
growth volatility only through the trade structure it induces. We then
re-estimate the second stage on the extended panel and compare the
concentration coefficient across the two sample periods.

\section{Data}
Export concentration is measured by the Herfindahl index over
four-digit product lines from the UN Comtrade database. GDP growth and
its within-country variance are computed from the World Bank national
accounts. The extended panel covers thirty-one economies over
1995--2022, of which the last decade is new relative to the original
study.

\section{Results}
On the original sample window our estimates line up closely with the
published ones, which validates the replication of the specification.
On the extended panel the coefficient roughly halves, and the
attenuation is driven almost entirely by the post-2011 years. The
mechanism appears to be the diversification that followed the commodity
price collapse rather than any change in measurement.

\section{Conclusion}
The headline finding survives replication on its own sample but
weakens considerably once the panel is extended past the commodity
boom. Policy conclusions drawn from the earlier window should be
tempered accordingly.

\bibliographystyle{plain}
\bibliography{refs}
\end{document}
